newsitem.title: UK: English Appeal Court quashes murder convictions.
newsitem.headline: English Appeal Court quashes murder convictions.

text.p: Three men who spent 18 years in prison for the murder of a newspaper delivery boy were exonerated on Wednesday, closing one of England's most infamous cases of miscarriage of justice.

The Court of Appeal quashed the convictions of Michael Hickey, his cousin Vincent, James Robinson and a fourth defendant Patrick Molloy, who died in prison, for the murder of 13-year-old Carl Bridgewater, shot dead during a robbery in 1978.
"We have concluded that the appellants did not have a fair trial and for that reason have quashed their convictions," Lord Justice John Roch told the court.
"This is another case of a miscarriage of justice which is a matter of regret for this court," he added.

Molloy, convicted of manslaughter, died of a brain haemorrhage in 1981, aged 57. The other three men were released on unconditional bail in February after prosecution lawyers said their trial was fundamentally flawed and the convictions unsafe.
The men, known as the Bridgewater Four, had always protested their innocence and had staged rooftop protests and hunger strikes during their long imprisonment.

During the four-week appeal hearing lawyer Michael Mansfield accused police of tricking Molloy into signing a false confession and said a squad of police officers had conducted a carefully cultivated strategy of deception.
The Appeal Court ruled that Molloy's confession had probably been obtained by deceit and was inadmissable.
Roch also noted new evidence showing that fingerprints obtained from Bridgewater's bicycle could not be matched to any of the convicted men.
He said it was not up to the court to decide their guilt or innocence, but to rule on the safety of their convictions.
"There are lessons for all of us who are involved in criminal justice to learn," he told the court.
The trio's exoneration is the latest black mark on England's criminal justice system.

It follows a series of wrongful imprisonment cases dating back to the 1970s including the "Guildford Four" and the "Birmingham Six" who were released from long prison sentences after being wrongly convicted of Irish Republican Army bombings on pubs that killed 36 people.
Ann Whelan, whose son Michael Hickey was too ill to attend court, said he had nothing but loathing for the justice system.

"(Michael) trusts nobody in it and I am not surprised. We should be talking to the police and saying get out there and find the real perpetrator of this crime and then maybe my lad will have some quality of life," she told reporters outside the court.
